As global ambient temperatures continue to rise, with the highest recorded annual averages since 1850 being within the last ten years, problems emerge for species exhibiting temperature-dependent sex determination. This is the process by which the sex of an animal’s embryo is determined based on the temperature of environment in which it is incubated, which can result in skewed sex ratios within a population like in the case of the critically endangered Hawksbill Sea Turtles (Eretmochelys imbricata). Reportedly, 85-95% of Hawksbills sampled in the wild are currently female [3]. This sex-imbalance can negatively impact the species’ ability to procreate, leading to the potential for extinction. Currently, no viable, long-term solutions exist to effectively and safely cool sea turtle eggs while still keeping them within their natural habitat. This research proposes the creation of sea turtle egg incubators designed to achieve a temperature range that will produce a higher percentage of male hatchlings to help rectify this imbalance in habitats heavily affected by climate change. These incubators are designed to be affordable, easy to build and, most importantly, safe for the sea turtle eggs. Three-month-long temperature trials for the incubator were conducted in Jamaica with conservationist community partners at Oracabessa Bay Sea Turtle Project. Results showed that this incubator is not only easy to manufacture and use, but that it successfully regulates the temperature range in favor of more male hatchlings, while also increasing the emergence rate of the hatchlings from 70% in natural nests to over 80%. During one of the hottest months in Jamaica, the incubator, deployed without water changes, doubled the predicted percentage of males produced by natural nests. When provided with cool water changes the incubator quintupled this value. Throughout the months of August to October, the incubator achieved a temperature range that is predicted to produce 85-99% male hatchlings, thus counteracting the feminization phenomenon occurring in nature.

We introduce a unified framework that connects regularized spectral dilation operators to a hybrid Mother–Ghost detection scheme for the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function. The construction is organized into three strictly separated layers: a black arithmetic core (the L-function and its zeros), a gray spectral scaffolding (a regularized dilation operator 𝒟_ε and its Mellin symbol), and a white observational apparatus (the Functional Mother Framework with SCD coherence). We present numerical evidence that a super-quintic reformulation of the spectral rigidity yields a 4× enhancement in phase stability at the critical line σ = 1/2, together with a 17.6× amplification under von Mangoldt weighting and a 2.5× circularity measure. We emphasize that this framework operates as a local-asymptotic spectral detector, not as a global proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. A closure principle is formulated to guarantee that observer-dependent moduli cannot alter intrinsic arithmetic facts. 1. Introduction The Hilbert–Pólya conjecture posits that the imaginary parts of the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function correspond to the eigenvalues of an unbounded self-adjoint operator on a suitable Hilbert space [4]. While no such operator has been constructed whose spectrum reproduces the zeta zeros exactly, a family of regularized dilation operators provides a controlled approximation in the limit of vanishing regularization. In parallel, the Functional Mother Framework (FMF) and its Structural Coherence Detector (SCD) have been developed as numerical probes that correlate deep minima in a regularized spectral response with the location of zeta zeros [author archive]. The purpose of this paper is to reconcile these two lines of investigation into a single mathematical structure with strict epistemic boundaries. To this end, we adopt a color-coded layer system: - Black: Intrinsic arithmetic objects. These exist independently of any regularization, representation, or observer choice. - Gray: Spectral scaffolding. These are regularization-dependent constructs necessary to build a spectral model, but they are not observational moduli. - White: Observational apparatus. These are tunable parameters of the measurement protocol; changing them changes the view, not the underlying arithmetic. The central result is that the gray layer—the dilation operator 𝒟_ε and its associated Bessel-channel rigidity—provides a natural spectral landscape upon which the white observational layer operates. Numerical experiments at ε ∈ {0.01, 0.02} with truncation N ≤ 10⁴ demonstrate quantitative discriminatory power favoring the critical line σ = 1/2. We explicitly state that these results constitute strong local-asymptotic evidence, not a global proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. 2. The non-trivial zeros are denoted: 𝒵 = {ρ ∈ ℂ : ζ(ρ) = 0, 0 < Re(ρ) < 1}. By the explicit formula of Riemann and von Mangoldt, the zeros are in duality with the primes through Λ(n) [1, 6]. The black layer is complete: it contains ζ(s), Λ(n), the set 𝒵, and all number-theoretic relations among them. No regularization parameter ε, no kernel K{ξ,κ}, and no truncation N appears here. 3.
